summary: Describes the problems of carrying IPv4 and IPv6 over IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) wireless broadband networks, pointing out gaps in the link layer's MAC design. It gives an overview of 802.16 network characteristics and convergence sublayers, and sets common terminology and goals for later solution documents. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5154 explains why running IP over an IEEE 802.16 wireless link is awkward. The wireless link is a set of separate point-to-point connections, while IP expects a shared network with broadcast and address lookup. The document sets out the choices available and the problems each one causes.

questions: why is wimax hard for ip
subtitle: Why carrying IP over a WiMAX link is harder than it looks, and what has to be fixed.

tldr.problem: The IEEE 802.16 MAC is connection-oriented and point-to-point, while IP assumes a shared subnet with broadcast, multicast and address resolution. Something has to give.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes the MAC layer and its convergence sublayers, then works through the three possible IP subnet models and the problems each creates, and states six goals for the IETF work that follows.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that the point-to-point link model is the right one for the IP convergence sublayer and the Ethernet-like model for the Ethernet sublayer, with multicast and broadcast traffic kept to a minimum.

today: RFC 5154 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It is the problem statement and set of goals for the IETF work on IP over IEEE 802.16, written by the problem statement team of the 16ng Working Group.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Broadband wireless access networks exist to fix the shortcomings of low bandwidth wireless communication for requirements such as high quality data and voice service, fast mobility and wide coverage. The IEEE 802.16 Working Group on Broadband Wireless Access develops standards and recommended practices for broadband wireless metropolitan area networks. The WiMAX Forum, and in particular its Network Working Group, defines the IEEE 802.16 network architecture, covering IPv4, IPv6, mobility, interworking, and authentication and authorization. WiBro, a Korean effort working in the 2.3 GHz band, is also based on the IEEE 802.16 specification.

IEEE 802.16 is point-to-point and connection-oriented at the MAC, physically arranged in a point-to-multipoint structure with the Base Station (BS) terminating one end of each connection and an individual Subscriber Station (SS) terminating the other. The convergence sublayer (CS) is the uppermost part of the MAC and assigns transmit-direction Service Data Units, originating from a higher layer application such as IP or Ethernet at the BS or SS, to a specific outbound transport connection. IEEE 802.16 defines two convergence sublayer types, the ATM Convergence Sublayer and the Packet CS. The IP Specific Subpart and the 802.3 Ethernet Specific Subpart of the Packet CS are within the scope of the IETF work described here.

Configuring an IP Subnet over such a network is complicated by the point-to-point, connection-oriented nature of the MAC and by the existence of both an IP CS and an Ethernet CS, which assume different higher-layer functionality. An IP Subnet is a topological area that uses the same IP address prefix, where that prefix is not further subdivided except into individual addresses. The IP CS assumes IP routing functionality in the upper layer, while the Ethernet CS assumes bridging functionality, so the characteristics of the link layer beneath IP change with the convergence sublayer chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: IEEE 802.16, the family of standards behind WiMAX broadband wireless, works as a set of separate point-to-point links, one per subscriber device. IP does not work that way. IP expects a shared network in which every device can reach the others by broadcast and look up their hardware addresses. This document works out what has to change on each side to make the two fit.

sections.title: The MAC Layer and Its Convergence Sublayers
sections.content:
Each SS has a 48-bit MAC address, and the BS has a 48-bit unique identifier called BSId. The two learn each other's address during the SS's entry into the network. The BS may also have a 48-bit MAC address, but that is known to the SS only when the Ethernet CS is used.

User data in both the uplink and the downlink direction is carried on unidirectional transport connections, each with parameters describing characteristics such as the cryptographic suite and quality of service. After a successful entry, no data traffic is possible, because no transport connection exists yet. Transport connections are established by a 3-message signaling sequence within the MAC layer, usually initiated by the BS. A downlink connection counts as multicast when it has been made available through MAC signaling to more than one SS; uplink connections are always unicast. Each transport connection is uniquely identified by a 16-bit connection identifier (CID).

An IEEE 802.16 PDU, the format transmitted over the airlink, consists of a Generic MAC header, various optional subheaders and a data payload. The Generic MAC header carries the CID of the connection the PDU belongs to. There is no source or destination address in the raw IEEE 802.16 MAC header.

The convergence sublayer maps between the MAC service and the internal connection-oriented service of the MAC Common Part Sublayer, through classification and encapsulation. It keeps an ordered classifier table whose entries pair a classifier with a target CID. A classifier is a conjunction of one or more subclassifiers, each naming a packet field, such as the destination MAC address in an Ethernet frame or the Type of Service field of an IP datagram inside one, together with a value or range of values. To classify an outbound SDU, the sublayer walks the table from the first entry to the last, and on a match associates the SDU with the target CID.

IEEE 802.16 defines the ATM CS and the Packet CS. The Packet CS has three subparts: the IP Specific Subpart, carrying IP packets over a point-to-point connection; the 802.3 Ethernet Specific Subpart, carrying packets in 802.3 format; and the 802.1Q VLAN Specific Subpart, carrying 802 style packets with VLAN tags. Unlike the Ethernet subpart, which has a classification that does not restrict the IP version, the IP and VLAN subparts classify strictly as either IPv4 or IPv6. An implementation may support several CS types at once, and the combination of CS type, subpart and classification defines the kind of data interface the higher layer sees.
sections.plainLanguage: The wireless link carries everything inside numbered connections, each with its own quality of service settings. The MAC header holds only the number of that connection, not an address. A convergence sublayer sits above the MAC and decides which connection each outgoing packet belongs in, by matching fields of the packet against a table of rules. The choice of sublayer decides whether the network above sees IP packets or Ethernet frames.

sections.title: The Root Problem: Choosing an IP Subnet Model
sections.content:
The key issue when deploying IP over IEEE 802.16 is how to configure an IP Subnet over a link that is connection-oriented and point-to-point at the MAC level. Three IP Subnet models are possible. In the point-to-point link model, each SS under a BS resides on a different IP Subnet, so only a certain SS and an access router (AR) exist under an IP Subnet, and IP packets with a link-local destination address are delivered only within the point-to-point link between the SS and the AR. PPP has been widely used for such links, but its direct use is not possible on IEEE 802.16 because the standard defines no convergence sublayer that encapsulates and decapsulates PPP frames. A mechanism is therefore needed to provide a point-to-point link between an SS and an AR when the IP CS is used. The alternative is PPP over Ethernet using the Ethernet CS, but the Ethernet CS assumes the upper layer provides bridging functionality to realize the Ethernet-like link model.

In the Ethernet-like link model, all SSs under an AR reside on the same IP Subnet, which also applies when the SSs are connected to different BSs. The model assumes the underlying link layer provides Ethernet-like functionality, such as native broadcast and multicast. Applying the Ethernet CS to configure this model seems feasible, but the IEEE 802.16 MAC is still connection-oriented and provides no multicast or broadcast connection for IP packet transfer, so a mechanism like IEEE 802.1D is needed to realize multicast and broadcast. Frequent IP multicast and broadcast signalling should be avoided, so that SSs in sleep or idle mode are not woken up.

The shared IPv6 prefix link model eventually results in multi-link subnet problems. The BS assigns separate IEEE 802.16 connections for the SSs, so the SSs are placed on different links, and distributing a shared IPv6 prefix across stations on different links causes multi-link subnet problems. This applies to the IP CS and even to the Ethernet CS if no bridging functionality is implemented on top of the BS or between the BS and the AR.

The feasible model therefore follows from the convergence sublayer: the point-to-point link model for the IP CS, and the Ethernet-like link model for the Ethernet CS, in which unnecessary multicast and broadcast packets within an IP Subnet should be minimized.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to arrange the IP addressing over the wireless network. Each device on its own subnet, all devices sharing one subnet, or all devices sharing one IPv6 prefix. Only the first two work, and which one works depends on whether the network above presents IP packets or Ethernet frames.

sections.title: Point-to-Point Link Model for IP CS: Problems
sections.content:
On address resolution, the IEEE 802.16 MAC address is not used as part of the 802.16 frame, so the usual Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) or neighbor cache does not apply and performing address resolution would be redundant. For IPv4, ARP cannot be carried by the IP CS at all, so it is not used by either the SS or the BS. For IPv6, address resolution is a function of the IP layer, with reachability state maintained through neighbour discovery packets, so blocking neighbour discovery packets would break the neighbour unreachability detection model.

On router discovery, the BS needs to send a Router Advertisement with a separate IP prefix, in unicast manner, for each SS, so that it can send periodic router advertisements in IEEE 802.16 networks. On prefix assignment, a separate IP prefix should be distributed for each SS so they can be located on different IP Subnets, and when an SS moves between BSs under the same AR, the AR needs to redistribute the same prefix the SS used at the previous BS.

On next-hop, the SS's next hop always needs to be the AR that provides IP connectivity in that access network. On neighbour unreachability detection, because the SS always sees an AR as the next hop, the detection is required only for that AR, and the requirement may depend on the existence of a connection to the BS for that destination. On address autoconfiguration, because a unique prefix is assigned to each SS, the IP Subnet contains only one SS and an AR, so duplicate address detection is trivial.
sections.plainLanguage: With one device per subnet, most of the usual IP machinery falls away. There is no need to look up hardware addresses, the device has only one possible neighbour to check for unreachability, and checking for a duplicate address is trivial because nobody else is on the subnet.

sections.title: Ethernet-Like Link Model for Ethernet CS: Problems
sections.content:
On address resolution, the sender must fill in the destination Ethernet address field even though that address is not used to transmit an 802.16 frame over the air. The Ethernet destination address is what a BS or bridge uses to decide where to forward the frame after decapsulating it. When the destination's IP address shares the sender's prefix, the sender should set the destination address to the destination itself, which requires conventional broadcast or multicast address resolution through ARP or the Neighbour Discovery Protocol. Unless these packets are filtered, as described in RFC 4541, the multicast and broadcast traffic wakes up SSs that are in sleep or idle mode.

On router discovery, all SSs under the AR are in the same broadcast domain, so sending periodic Router Advertisements to the all-nodes multicast address has the same effect of waking sleeping SSs. On prefix assignment, the same IP prefix is shared with multiple SSs, so an IP Subnet holds several SSs and an AR. The SS assumes that on-link neighbours exist and tries to resolve the layer 2 address for the on-link prefixes, but direct communication between two SSs using link-layer addresses is not possible with the Ethernet CS alone; bridging functionality must be added on top of the BS or between the BS and the AR.

On next-hop, when the Ethernet CS is used and the accompanying Ethernet capability emulation is implemented, the next hop for a destination IP that shares the sender's global prefix, or is of link-local address type, should be the destination itself rather than an AR. On neighbour unreachability detection, all SSs under the same AR are neighbours, so detection is required for all of them and for the AR. On address autoconfiguration, duplicate address detection should be performed among the multiple SSs and the AR sharing the prefix, and the previous multicast-based method has the same problem of waking sleeping SSs.
sections.plainLanguage: With every device on one shared subnet, the devices must behave like they are on an Ethernet cable. That means broadcasts, address lookups and duplicate address checks, and each of those travels to every device, including the ones whose screens are off and whose batteries matter.

sections.title: Goals and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document states six goals for the work to be done in the IETF. Goal one is to define the way to provide the point-to-point link model for the IP CS. Goal two is to reduce the power consumption caused by waking up sleep or idle terminals for the Ethernet-like link model. Goal three is to avoid multi-link subnet problems. Goal four is to allow the applicability of security schemes such as SEcure Neighbor Discovery, RFC 3971. Goal five is to introduce no new security threats. Goal six is to review management requirements, and in particular the interfaces and the specific management model objects for IP over IEEE 802.16, in collaboration with the IEEE 802.16 working group.

The security considerations section says the document describes a problem statement and goals for IP over IEEE 802.16 networks and introduces no new security threats. The IEEE 802.16 link layer employs the cryptographic security mechanisms it specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: The work that follows has six targets: make the point-to-point model work for IP, stop the shared model from waking sleeping devices, avoid the multi-link subnet problem, keep secure neighbour discovery usable, add no new security exposure, and settle the management interfaces with the IEEE working group.
